questions.question: In a patient with prior TAVI who presents with dyspnoea, dizziness, and fatigue, what echocardiographic findings in this case established severe prosthetic aortic valve dysfunction before the third intervention?

What are the major causes of failure of a transcatheter aortic bioprosthesis, and how did this patient’s prior Enterococcus faecalis prosthetic valve endocarditis likely contribute to later restenosis and regurgitation?

In a patient with recurrent dysfunction after two prior transcatheter aortic valves, what differential diagnosis should be considered for elevated transvalvular gradients and new regurgitation, and which features in this case argued against active infective endocarditis at the time of the third procedure?

Why is preprocedural CT especially important in TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV planning, and which specific anatomic measurements and relationships were used in this case to assess feasibility and the risk of coronary obstruction?
What factors made this patient a poor candidate for surgical explantation and redo valve surgery, despite guideline preference for surgery in many cases of prosthetic valve endocarditis?
Why was a self-expanding Acurate neo2 chosen as the third prosthesis in this case, and what design features made it attractive in the setting of a narrow, triple-stented aortic valve anatomy?

What was the rationale for high implantation of the third valve at the level of the Evolut leaflets, and how can this strategy improve effective orifice area while helping preserve coronary flow and future coronary access?

Immediately after the third TAVI, the mean gradient remained high at 67 mm Hg with an indexed AVA of 0.4 cm²/m² and DVI of 0.24. How would you interpret these findings, and what explains the subsequent improvement in haemodynamics over the following month?
